promise: After this you can explain what an index is, what it costs, and how B-tree and search indexes differ.

terms.definition: Reading every row to find the ones you want, slow when the table is large.
Finding the rows that match a condition, such as all orders for one customer.
A unit of text to search, such as one web page, email, or product description.

before.note: Read Databases and Sharding first: an index speeds lookups within a database, and search spreads indexes across shards. The terms below are enough to begin.

stages.name: Basics
body: Without help, finding rows that match a condition means reading every row, a full table scan, which gets slow as the table grows. PostgreSQL's page says that without an index the system would have to scan the entire table row by row, which is clearly inefficient when only a few rows are returned. An index lets it jump to matching rows instead, the same idea as the alphabetic index at the back of a book, which the page itself uses as its comparison [[pg-indexes-intro]].

An index trades write cost for read speed. After an index is created the system has to keep it synchronised with the table, which the page says adds overhead to data manipulation operations, and indexes that are seldom or never used in queries should be removed [[pg-indexes-intro]]. In return, the right query becomes dramatically faster. Deciding which indexes to keep is a balance between faster reads and slower writes.

Search engines generalise the same idea to text. Instead of scanning every document for a word, they build an inverted index that maps each word to the list of documents containing it. Lucene's documentation says its core, the inverted index, is made of postings, which with their term dictionary work as a map from a term to the ordered list of documents containing it [[lucene-index]].

terms.definition: An ordered structure beside the data that lets the database find matching rows without scanning all of them.
Reading every row to answer a query, the slow fallback when no index helps.
A map from each term to the list of documents that contain it, the core of text search.
How few rows a condition matches; an index helps most when a query is selective.
The extra write work indexes add, since each must be updated on every change.

reading.what: What an index is, why it avoids scanning every row, and that it adds overhead to data changes.
How the inverted index maps a term to the documents containing it.

canNow: Explain why a table scan gets slow and how an index avoids it.
State the trade-off an index makes.
Say what an inverted index maps and why search uses it.

stages.name: How it works
body: PostgreSQL's page says that by default CREATE INDEX creates a B-tree index, which fits the most common situations, and that B-trees can handle equality and range queries on data that can be sorted. It offers other types too: hash, GiST, SP-GiST, GIN and BRIN [[pg-indexes-types]].

The index type must match the query. The page says hash indexes can only handle simple equality comparisons. Choosing the type is choosing which queries get fast; each type uses a different algorithm that is best suited to different indexable clauses [[pg-indexes-types]].

Text search needs more than exact matching. Elasticsearch describes text analysis as converting unstructured text into a structured format optimised for search. It breaks text into tokens, which are usually individual words, and normalises them, for example lowercasing and reducing foxes to its root fox, and it applies the same rules to the query string. Analysis happens when indexing or searching text fields [[es-analysis]].

A relevant point for scale: Elasticsearch divides each index into shards and distributes them across the nodes in your cluster, which lets an index handle large volumes of traffic [[es-docs]]. A search across shards has to ask every shard and merge the results, which is general practice rather than something that page spells out.

terms.definition: A balanced, sorted tree index that serves both equality and range queries efficiently.
An index that answers equality lookups quickly but cannot do ranges.
Breaking text into terms, the first step in building a searchable inverted index.
Normalizing tokens, such as lowercasing and reducing words to a root, so related words match.
The inverted index one shard keeps over its own documents, queried in parallel with the others.

reading.what: Which kinds of comparison each index type can serve.
How text is broken into tokens and normalised so a search can match related words.

canNow: Say what a B-tree index does and why it is the default.
Match an index type to a query shape.
Explain tokenization and analysis in text search.

stages.name: Going deeper
body: A query often filters on several columns, and the order of columns in a multicolumn index matters. PostgreSQL's page says a multicolumn B-tree index can be used with conditions on any subset of its columns, but the index is most efficient when there are constraints on the leading, leftmost columns. Getting this order wrong is why an index that looks relevant may not help the query you actually run [[pg-indexes-multicolumn]].

The database does not use an index just because one exists; the query planner decides. PostgreSQL says the system will use the index in queries when it thinks that would be more efficient than a sequential table scan, and that you may need to run ANALYZE regularly so the planner has statistics to decide with. Reading the chosen plan is how you learn whether your index is actually helping [[pg-indexes-intro]].

Search ranks rather than just matches. Lucene's similarity classes score the matching documents so the most relevant come first. Its documentation describes BM25Similarity, with a parameter that calibrates term frequency saturation, scoring that also uses the IDF of the matched terms, and ClassicSimilarity, the original Lucene scoring function based on the vector space model and TF-IDF [[lucene-similarities]].

terms.definition: An index over several columns; the column order decides which queries it can serve.
A composite index helps queries that use its first columns, not ones that skip them.
Answering a query from the index alone, without touching the table, when the index holds every needed column.
Ranking matching documents so the most relevant appear first.
Scoring that rewards a term appearing often in a document but being rare across all documents.

reading.what: Why column order in a multicolumn index decides how efficient it is.
How Lucene scores matching documents with BM25 and with classic TF-IDF.

canNow: Explain why column order in a composite index matters.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: Every index is a bet: it speeds some queries while slowing all writes and taking space. The practical discipline is to index for the queries you actually run, confirm with the query plan that each index is used, and drop ones that are not. An unused index is pure cost. PostgreSQL devotes a whole section to examining whether your indexes are being used and refining them against the real workload [[pg-indexes-examine]].

Databases and search engines make different default bargains. A relational B-tree index favours exact and range lookups on structured columns; a search engine favours flexible text matching and ranking, and it updates its index slightly behind the source data. Elasticsearch says a stored document is fully searchable in near real-time, within one second, because a refresh makes recent changes visible, by default every second [[es-near-real-time]]. Many systems use both: the database as the source of truth, a search index kept in sync beside it.

At scale the two topics meet. A sharded database spreads rows across shards, and a search cluster spreads its inverted index across shards the same way. Running each query on every shard and merging the results is general practice, not something the cited page spells out. The indexing ideas here are what make queries fast within each shard, so this topic completes the data path the earlier topics built [[es-docs]].

terms.definition: The actual set of queries an app runs, which should drive which indexes exist.
An index no query uses; it costs storage and write time for no benefit.
The authoritative store, often a database, with a search index kept in sync beside it.
A search index that reflects new data after a short delay rather than instantly.

misconceptions.myth: More indexes always make a database faster.
misconceptions.truth: Each index adds overhead to data manipulation operations, and PostgreSQL says indexes that are seldom or never used should be removed [[pg-indexes-intro]].

misconceptions.myth: An index on the right column is always used.
misconceptions.truth: The system uses an index when it thinks that is more efficient than a sequential scan, and a multicolumn index is most efficient on its leading columns [[pg-indexes-intro]] [[pg-indexes-multicolumn]].

misconceptions.myth: Full-text search is just a LIKE query on steroids.
misconceptions.truth: Elasticsearch breaks text into tokens and normalises them before indexing, and Lucene's inverted index maps each term to the documents containing it [[es-analysis]] [[lucene-index]].

misconceptions.myth: A search index is always perfectly in sync with the database.
misconceptions.truth: Elasticsearch calls its search near real-time: document changes are not visible to search immediately but within about a second [[es-near-real-time]].

tryIt.intro: These inspect indexing in a PostgreSQL database with psql. The statements and the table names test1 and tenk1 are examples from the PostgreSQL pages cited below, so use tables of your own. Output depends on your data, so it is not shown here.

commands.shows: Builds an index on the id column of the page's example table test1. The page says the index name can be chosen freely.
commands.warning: This builds an index, which can take a long time on a large table and blocks writes to it while it runs. Run it only on a test database.

commands.command: CREATE INDEX test2_mm_idx ON test2 (major, minor);
commands.shows: A multicolumn index on two columns of the page's example table test2.
commands.warning: This builds an index on a table. Run it only on a test database.

commands.command: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM tenk1 WHERE unique1 < 100;
commands.shows: The plan chosen for a restrictive condition. The page's example output uses a bitmap index scan on tenk1; EXPLAIN shows the plan without running the query.
